title: Evals: proving your AI feature works
summary: How to test a feature whose output changes every time: a test set, graders in code and by model, a score, and a check that runs on every change.
youWillLearn: Why "it worked when I tried it" is not testing for AI features
How to build a small test set that covers the cases that break
When to grade with code and when with an LLM judge
How to catch regressions before they ship, in CI

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.Claude API: Anthropic's AI, reached over the internet: you send it text, it sends text back. Each call costs a little money.
glossary.eval: An automated test for an AI feature: run a fixed set of inputs through it, grade each output, and get a score.
glossary.test set: The fixed list of inputs (and what you expect from them) that an eval runs every time.
glossary.grader: The check that decides whether one output passes: a piece of code, a model with a rubric, or a person.
glossary.LLM judge: Using a model, with a clear rubric, to grade another model's output on qualities code cannot check, such as faithfulness.
glossary.rubric: A short list of specific pass/fail criteria that a grader applies to each output.
glossary.regression: Something that used to work and broke after a change.
glossary.baseline: The score of the current version, which every change is compared against.
glossary.pull request: A proposed change to the code, reviewed before it is merged into the main version.
glossary.CI: Continuous integration: checks that run automatically on every pull request, for example in GitHub Actions.

steps.title: You test prompts by trying them
body: Notely, our notes app, summarizes notes for users like Maya. The app server (the computer running Notely's code) sends each note to the Claude API, Anthropic's AI, with the summary prompt from lesson 3.
When you change that prompt, you try a note or two by hand, then ship. Nobody knows the real pass rate.

scene.caption: Maya's notes go through the app server to Claude and come back summarized.

steps.title: Fixed one note, broke three others
body: Spanish notes were getting English summaries, so you changed the prompt. You tried one Spanish note. Perfect. Shipped.
A week later Maya complains: summaries of long notes stopped mentioning decisions. Nobody tried long notes. Model output varies, so a few tries by hand prove very little.
changes: ~ App Server: runs prompt version 2
~ Maya: long summaries lost their decisions

scene.caption: The fix worked for one note and quietly broke another kind.

steps.title: Same inputs, graded, every time
body: An eval is a test for output that varies. Take a fixed test set, run each input through the real feature, let a grader mark each output pass or fail, and add up the score.
Rerun it after every prompt or model change. The question becomes: did the score go up or down, and which cases changed?

callout.text: A design crit with a fixed checklist and the same ten screens every week. Opinions vary; the checklist makes changes visible.

changes: − Maya: evals run before users see anything
+ Test Set and Grader: fixed inputs, marked pass or fail
~ Cases tested 1 → 60
~ Pass rate – → 75%

scene.caption: Sixty fixed notes go through the real feature, and each answer gets graded.

steps.title: Build the test set from what breaks
body: Start small: 30 to 100 cases beat zero. Use realistic notes, made up or real ones with consent and personal details removed, and add the awkward ones on purpose.
Empty notes. Huge notes. Other languages. Pasted emails. Notes that try to give the model orders. Every bug a user ever reported. Each case says what a good answer must have.

code.caption: One case per line, kept in the repo next to the prompt it tests.

changes: ~ Test Set: filled with edge cases and past bugs
~ Grader steps back

scene.caption: The test set holds the cases most likely to break.

steps.title: Grade with code wherever you can
body: Many checks need no AI at all. Three bullets or fewer? Does it contain the words this case requires? Is it the exact "too short" reply for an empty note?
Code graders are free, instant, and give the same verdict every time. Write as many as you can before reaching for anything fancier.

code.caption: Format, length, required words: all checked by plain code.

changes: ~ Grader: plain code checks format, length, words
~ Test Set steps back

scene.caption: The first grader is ordinary code.

steps.title: A model as judge, with a rubric
body: Some qualities code cannot check: is every claim actually in the note? Is the key decision there? Use an LLM judge: a separate Claude call with the note, the summary and a strict rubric.
Ask for pass or fail per point, not a score out of ten. Grade 20 outputs by hand to check the judge agrees.

code.code:
You grade a summary of a note. For each point, answer PASS or FAIL.
1. Every fact in the summary appears in the note.
2. The note's main decision, if any, is included.
3. It is written in the same language as the note.
Explain briefly, then give the three verdicts.
code.caption: Get the verdicts back as structured output (lesson 4), so the runner can count them.

changes: ~ Grader: also asks Claude to judge, with a rubric
~ Claude API: second job as the judge
~ Pass rate 75 → 70%: the judge catches invented facts

scene.caption: The grader sends hard questions to a separate judge call.

steps.title: Catch regressions before they ship
body: Today's score is the baseline. A lower score, or a case that passed and now fails, is a regression.

Run the eval in CI (checks that run automatically) on every pull request (a proposed code change, before it is merged) that touches prompts or models. Prompt v3 scores 65% against a 70% baseline: CI blocks it.

callout.text: Evals call the model, so they cost money. Run the full set on prompt changes and before releases, not on every commit to every file.

changes: + CI: runs the eval on every pull request
~ Pass rate 70 → 65%: below the baseline
~ App Server: tries prompt version 3
~ Grader and Claude API step back

scene.caption: CI runs the eval and refuses a change that scores lower.

steps.title: Notely's eval runner
body: The runner is a small script. It loads the cases, calls the same summarize function the app uses, grades each output, prints the failures, and fails CI if the score drops.
No framework needed to start. Eval tools add dashboards and history later; the idea stays this simple. You fix the prompt, and the score climbs.

code.caption: The runner tests the real function, so it can never drift from what users get.

changes: ~ App Server: prompt version 4, the fix
~ CI: passes after the prompt fix
~ Pass rate 65 → 88%
~ Grader and Claude API back in view

scene.caption: Cases in, real feature, graded, scored: the whole loop in one script.

steps.title: Evals rot unless you feed them
body: Output varies, so one run can pass by luck: run key cases several times. And do not tune the prompt until the set passes and stop there. That is overfitting, and real users bring new cases.
Feed the set from real use: every thumbs-down, complaint or odd log from Maya and friends becomes a new case.

callout.text: When Claude Code "fixes" a prompt, ask it to run the eval and show before/after per case, not one example. Check the diff: did it edit or delete test cases to make them pass? Does the eval call the real app function?

changes: + Maya: her thumbs-down becomes a new test case
~ Cases tested 60 → 64
~ Pass rate 88 → 84%: new cases are hard ones

scene.caption: Real complaints flow into the test set, so it keeps up with real use.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: AI output varies, so trying it by hand proves little. An eval runs a fixed test set through the real feature, grades each output, and gives a score.
Grade with code first, use an LLM judge with a pass/fail rubric for the rest, compare with the baseline in CI, and keep feeding the set with real failures.
changes: ~ Every part working together: cases, grader, CI

scene.caption: Test set, real feature, graders, CI, and real failures flowing back in.

quiz.question: Which check is best done by code instead of an LLM judge?

options.text: Does the summary have three bullets or fewer?
options.why: Counting is exact, free and instant in code. Save the judge for qualities code cannot measure.

options.text: Is every fact in the summary supported by the note?
options.why: That needs reading comprehension. It is a classic job for a judge model with a rubric.

options.text: Does the summary capture the note's main decision?
options.why: Spotting the main decision takes understanding. A code check would miss rephrasings.

quiz.question: A prompt change raises the eval score from 54 to 56 out of 60, but two cases that used to pass now fail. What do you do?

options.text: Merge it: the score went up.
options.why: A higher total can hide a new break. The two new failures might matter more than the four new passes.

options.text: Look at the two new failures before deciding.
options.why: Per-case changes are the point of an eval. A regression on an important case can outweigh a small gain elsewhere.

options.text: Delete the two failing cases, since they look flaky.
options.why: That hides a regression. If a case is truly flaky, run it several times, but do not drop it to make the number look good.

quiz.question: Claude Code says it improved the summary prompt and shows one great example output. What should you ask for?

options.why: Hand-picked examples are still anecdotes. They do not show what broke elsewhere.

options.text: A switch to a bigger model, to be safe.
options.why: That changes cost and still proves nothing. Measure first.

options.text: The eval results before and after, per case, with the test file untouched.
options.why: Only the full set shows gains and regressions, and an untouched test file proves the cases were not bent to pass.

takeaways: An eval = fixed test set + grader + score, run on every prompt or model change.
Build the test set from edge cases and past bugs, then keep adding real failures from users.
Grade with code first. Use an LLM judge with a pass/fail rubric for faithfulness, and check it against your own grading.
Compare each run with the baseline per case, in CI, before merging.
Ask Claude Code for before/after eval results, never one hand-picked example.
